summary: Sea Level is assumed to be Y = 63 in numerous parts of Minecraft
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Launch Minecraft and create a new Singleplayer Creative world with default settings.
2. Enter the world, then use the in-game "Esc menu -> Save and Quit to Title".
3. Select the world and open "Singleplayer -> [world] -> Edit -> Open World Folder".
4. Copy the attached `TallOceansTest` datapack into the world's `datapacks` folder.
5. Reopen the world and travel to an ocean generated by the datapack.
6. Wait at least a few minutes for natural mob spawning to occur.
7. Observe that the ocean's water level is above Y 63, while the affected aquatic mobs do not spawn there as expected; other sea-level-dependent behavior, such as blue ice generation or ocean monument water placement, may also be inconsistent with the configured sea level.
8. Repeat steps 1–5 using the attached `SnowTestUnder63` datapack instead.
9. Observe that terrain and temperature-related behavior, including snow placement, still uses the vanilla Y 63/Y 64 assumptions even though the datapack configures a lower sea level.
Environment: Minecraft Java Edition Versions: 1.17 Pre-release 1, 1.17, 1.18 Pre-release 3, 1.18 Pre-release 4, 1.18.1, 22w12a, 1.19.2, 1.19.3, 23w07a, 1.20.2, 23w45a (includes snapshots)
Observed Behavior: When the chunk generator is configured with a sea level other than Y 63, many systems continue using the value returned by Level.getSeaLevel as though it were the generator’s actual sea level. Because this value is not synchronized with the chunk generator, aquatic mob spawning becomes incorrect. Dolphins, drowned, turtles, and squid may fail to spawn in ocean water when the configured sea level is above Y 63, while axolotls and glow squids may only spawn when the ocean floor is below Y 63. Ocelot spawn obstruction checks also use the incorrect level, causing spawning to be incorrectly allowed below an elevated sea level and incorrectly obstructed when the configured sea level is below Y 63. Phantom anchor points are clamped to Y 64 instead of to one block above the configured sea level, and phantom spawning rates or locations change incorrectly when the sea level differs from Y 63. Bats fail to spawn in caves below an elevated sea level and can spawn in areas where they should not when the configured sea level is lower. Drowned spawning uses a fixed effective threshold of Y 58 rather than five blocks below the configured sea level. The blue ice feature fails to generate in water bodies above Y 62, regardless of the configured sea level. Ocean monuments use hardcoded Y 64 behavior in OceanMonumentPieces.postProcess and related water-box generation, causing their placement and filling to disregard the chunk generator’s sea level and ocean-floor height. Ocean ruins similarly place air or water incorrectly around drowned data markers because their block replacement logic uses the unsynchronized sea-level value. Amphibious pathfinding for axolotls and turtles applies the shallow-water cost adjustment relative to the incorrect sea level, which can produce inaccurate paths when water is generated at different heights. Biome temperature adjustment also remains based on Y 64, causing temperature and snow behavior to be incorrect when the configured sea level is changed, particularly in the SnowTestUnder63 datapack. These problems can be reproduced with the attached TallOceansTest and SnowTestUnder63 datapacks and indicate that code relying on Level.getSeaLevel is not receiving the chunk generator’s configured sea level. The server-side level should obtain this value from the active chunk generator, and the corresponding sea-level information should also be made available to clients where client-side calculations require it.
Expected Behavior: All sea-level-dependent systems should use the chunk generator’s configured sea level rather than assuming Y=63. Mob spawning, obstruction checks, phantom behavior, pathfinding, blue ice and ocean feature generation, monument and ruin water placement, and biome temperature adjustments should remain correct when sea level is raised or lowered, with water, air, height thresholds, and environmental behavior consistently aligned to the configured value.
